entries.title: no such column
entries.explain: SQLite looked for this column in every table named in `FROM` and `JOIN` and found none with that name. The query is checked before it runs, so no rows were read.
causes: A typo, or the singular/plural form of the name (`user_id` vs `userid`).
The column belongs to a table that is not in the `FROM` or `JOIN` list.
A table alias that points at the wrong table: `o.name` where `o` is `orders`.
Text written without quotes, so SQLite reads it as a column name: `WHERE city = Paris`.
fix: Check the table's columns (`PRAGMA table_info(tablename);`) and fix the name.
Join the table that has the column, and qualify it with the right alias.
Put text values in single quotes: `WHERE city = 'Paris'`.
entries.before: SELECT name FROM users WHERE city = Paris;
entries.after: SELECT name FROM users WHERE city = 'Paris';
entries.specific: No table in this query has a column `{column}`{onLine}.

entries.title: no such table
entries.explain: The statement refers to a table (or view) that does not exist in this database.
causes: A typo, or singular/plural confusion (`user` vs `users`).
The `CREATE TABLE` statement has not run yet, or failed earlier.
The table is in a different database file, or in an in-memory database that was closed.
fix: List the tables to see the real names: `SELECT name FROM sqlite_schema WHERE type = 'table';`.
Run the `CREATE TABLE` before querying, and check it did not fail.
entries.before: SELECT * FROM user;
entries.after: SELECT * FROM users;
entries.specific: There is no table `{table}`{onLine}.

entries.title: near "...": syntax error
entries.explain: SQLite could not parse the statement. The word or symbol in quotes is where parsing failed; the actual mistake is often just before it.
causes: A misspelled keyword: `SELEC`, `FORM`, `WHER`.
A comma before `FROM` (`SELECT a, b, FROM t`) or a missing comma between columns.
A reserved word used as a name, such as a column called `order` or `group`.
Clauses in the wrong order: the order is `SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT`.
fix: Look at the quoted token and the word right before it.
Quote reserved words used as names with double quotes: `"order"`.
Put clauses in the standard order.
entries.before: SELECT name, email, FROM users;
entries.after: SELECT name, email FROM users;
entries.specific: Parsing failed at `{token}`{onLine}; check the text just before it.

entries.title: unrecognized token
entries.explain: SQLite found characters it cannot read as any piece of SQL. Most often a string literal was opened with `'` and never closed, so everything after it became one broken token.
causes: A missing closing `'` on a text value.
An apostrophe inside text: `'O'Brien'` (double it: `'O''Brien'`).
A character SQL does not use, such as a stray backslash or a smart quote pasted from a document.
fix: Close every string with `'`.
Write an apostrophe inside text as two: `'it''s'`.
From application code, pass values as parameters instead of pasting them into SQL.
entries.before: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Ann;
entries.after: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'Ann';
entries.specific: SQLite cannot read `{token}`{onLine}.

entries.title: incomplete input
entries.explain: The SQL text ended in the middle of a statement, so SQLite is still waiting for the rest, such as a closing parenthesis or the end of a clause.
causes: A missing `)` at the end of `CREATE TABLE (...)` or `VALUES (...)`.
A statement cut off after a keyword: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE`.
A `CREATE TRIGGER` without its closing `END;`.
fix: Finish the statement: close every parenthesis and complete the last clause.
entries.before:
CREATE TABLE items (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
entries.specific: The SQL ends before the statement is complete.

entries.title: ambiguous column name
entries.explain: More than one table in the query has a column with this name, so SQLite cannot tell which one you mean. This is common with `id` or `name` after a `JOIN`.
causes: Two joined tables both have the column (`users.id` and `orders.id`).
Using the bare name in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY` or `GROUP BY` after a join.
fix: Qualify the column with its table or alias: `u.id`, `o.id`.
Give tables short aliases in `FROM` to keep it readable.
entries.before:
SELECT id, total
FROM users JOIN orders ON orders.user_id = users.id;
entries.after:
SELECT u.id, o.total
FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
entries.specific: More than one table here has a column `{column}`{onLine}; say which one, like `table.{column}`.

entries.title: misuse of aggregate
entries.explain: Aggregate functions (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) summarize groups of rows, so they cannot appear where SQLite looks at one row at a time, such as in `WHERE`, and they cannot be nested directly inside each other.
causes: Filtering on an aggregate in `WHERE`: `WHERE COUNT(*) > 1`.
Nesting aggregates: `SUM(COUNT(*))`.
Using an aggregate inside a `JOIN ... ON` condition.
fix: Filter groups with `HAVING` after `GROUP BY`: `GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.
To aggregate an aggregate, compute the inner one in a subquery or CTE first.
entries.specific: `{func}()` is used{onLine} in a place that works row by row; use `HAVING` or a subquery.

entries.message: aggregate functions are not allowed in the GROUP BY clause
entries.title: aggregate functions are not allowed in the GROUP BY clause
entries.explain: `GROUP BY` decides which rows go together, so it must be based on values from each row. An aggregate such as `COUNT(*)` only exists after the groups are formed, so it cannot define them.
causes: Putting the aggregate itself in `GROUP BY`: `GROUP BY COUNT(*)`.
Grouping by a `SELECT` alias that refers to an aggregate.
fix: Group by the plain column (`GROUP BY city`) and keep the aggregate in `SELECT` or `HAVING`.
To group by an aggregate's result, compute it in a subquery first.
entries.before: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM users GROUP BY n;
entries.after: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS n FROM users GROUP BY city;
entries.specific: The `GROUP BY`{onLine} contains an aggregate.

entries.message: a GROUP BY clause is required before HAVING|HAVING clause on a non-aggregate query
entries.title: HAVING used without grouping
entries.explain: `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation. In a query with no `GROUP BY` and no aggregate functions there are no groups, so SQLite rejects it. Older SQLite versions also required `GROUP BY` before any `HAVING`.
causes: Using `HAVING` where `WHERE` was meant, to filter individual rows.
Forgetting the `GROUP BY` clause.
fix: Filter rows with `WHERE`.
Or add the `GROUP BY` that `HAVING` should work on.
entries.before: SELECT name FROM users HAVING age > 30;
entries.after: SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30;
entries.specific: The `HAVING`{onLine} has no groups to filter; use `WHERE` or add `GROUP BY`.

entries.title: UNIQUE constraint failed
entries.explain: The insert or update would give two rows the same value in a column (or combination of columns) that must be unique, such as a `PRIMARY KEY` or a `UNIQUE` column. SQLite rejected the change.
causes: Inserting a row with an explicit `id` that already exists.
Running the same `INSERT` twice.
Duplicate values (such as the same email) in the data.
fix: Leave out the `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` value so SQLite picks a new one.
Skip duplicates with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, or update instead with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET ...`.
Check for an existing row first.
entries.before:
INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Ann');
INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Bo');
entries.after:
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ann');
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Bo');
entries.specific: Another row already has this value in `{target}`{onLine}.

entries.title: NOT NULL constraint failed
entries.explain: The column is declared `NOT NULL`, and the insert or update would leave it `NULL`. Columns you leave out of an `INSERT` get their `DEFAULT`, which is `NULL` unless the table says otherwise.
causes: The column is missing from the `INSERT` column list and has no `DEFAULT`.
An explicit `NULL`, or a value that is `NULL` because it came from a failed lookup.
Values in the wrong order, so a `NULL` lands in the wrong column.
fix: Include the column with a real value.
Or give the column a default in the table: `status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'`.
entries.before:
CREATE TABLE tasks (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO tasks (id) VALUES (1);
entries.after:
CREATE TABLE tasks (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO tasks (id, title) VALUES (1, 'Write report');
entries.specific: `{target}` would be `NULL`{onLine}, which it does not allow.

entries.title: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
entries.explain: A foreign key says a value must match a row in another (parent) table. The change would leave a row pointing at a parent that does not exist, either by inserting a bad reference or by deleting a parent that still has children. SQLite does not say which key failed.
causes: Inserting a child row whose reference (`user_id = 99`) has no matching parent.
Inserting children before their parent row.
Deleting or changing a parent row that child rows still point to.
fix: Insert the parent row first, and use its real key in the child.
Delete the children first, or declare the key with `ON DELETE CASCADE` (or `SET NULL`) if that is the behaviour you want.
entries.before: INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES (99, 20);   -- no user 99
entries.after:
INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (99, 'Ann');
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES (99, 20);
entries.specific: A row{onLine} would point at a parent row that does not exist, or a parent still has children.

entries.title: CHECK constraint failed
entries.explain: The table has a `CHECK` rule that every row must satisfy, and the new or changed row breaks it. SQLite names the rule, or shows its expression.
causes: A value outside the allowed range, such as a negative price when the rule is `price > 0`.
Text that is not in the allowed list: `CHECK (status IN ('open', 'done'))`.
Values in the wrong column order, so a value ends up in a column with a rule.
fix: Change the value so it meets the rule.
If the rule is wrong, change the table definition (in SQLite that means recreating the table).
entries.before:
CREATE TABLE items (name TEXT, price REAL CHECK (price > 0));
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('pen', -1);
entries.after:
CREATE TABLE items (name TEXT, price REAL CHECK (price > 0));
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('pen', 1.5);
entries.specific: The row{onLine} breaks the rule `{check}`.

entries.title: datatype mismatch
entries.explain: SQLite is relaxed about column types, but a few places are strict: an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` column must hold an integer, and `STRICT` tables require each value to match its column type. A value of another type was stored there.
causes: Inserting text or a decimal into an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` column.
Inserting a value of the wrong type into a `STRICT` table.
fix: Store an integer in the key column, or leave it out so SQLite assigns one.
Convert values to the column's type first, for example `CAST('42' AS INTEGER)`.
entries.before:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO users VALUES ('a1', 'Ann');
entries.after:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ann');
entries.specific: A value{onLine} has the wrong type for its column.

entries.message: table (?<table>\S+) has (?<cols>\d+) columns but (?<vals>\d+) values were supplied|(?<vals>\d+) values for (?<cols>\d+) columns
entries.title: Number of values does not match number of columns
entries.explain: An `INSERT` must give exactly one value per column it fills. Without a column list, that means every column of the table, in order; with a column list, one value per listed column.
causes: `INSERT INTO t VALUES (...)` with fewer values than the table has columns (often leaving out the `id`).
A column list and a `VALUES` list of different lengths.
A missing comma that merges two values into one expression.
fix: Name the columns you are filling: `INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (...)`.
Make the value list match the column list one to one.
entries.before:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT);
INSERT INTO users VALUES ('Ann', 'ann@example.com');
entries.after:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT);
INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Ann', 'ann@example.com');
entries.specific: The `INSERT`{onLine} gives {vals} values for {cols} columns.

entries.title: table already exists
entries.explain: `CREATE TABLE` (or `CREATE INDEX` / `VIEW`) was run for a name that is already taken in this database, usually because the script ran before.
causes: Running a setup script a second time against the same database.
Two `CREATE` statements with the same name.
fix: Use `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ...` to make setup safe to repeat.
Or start fresh with `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS name;` first (this deletes its data).
entries.before: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
entries.after: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
entries.specific: A {kind} called `{name}` already exists{onLine}.

entries.title: duplicate column name
entries.explain: A table cannot have two columns with the same name. The `CREATE TABLE` lists it twice, or `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` adds a column that already exists.
causes: A copy-pasted column line in `CREATE TABLE`.
Running an `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` migration twice.
fix: Remove or rename the duplicate.
Check `PRAGMA table_info(name);` before adding a column in a migration.
entries.before: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, name TEXT);
entries.after: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT);
entries.specific: `{column}` is declared twice{onLine}.

entries.title: no such function
entries.explain: SQLite has no function with this name. Function names differ between databases: many from SQL Server, MySQL or PostgreSQL do not exist in SQLite, or are spelled differently.
causes: Functions from other databases: `LEN` (SQLite: `length`), `NOW()` / `GETDATE()` (SQLite: `datetime('now')`), `DATEDIFF` (SQLite: `julianday(a) - julianday(b)`), `ISNULL` (SQLite: `ifnull` or `coalesce`).
A typo in the function name.
Math functions such as `sqrt` or `pow`, which exist only when SQLite was built with them enabled.
fix: Use SQLite's equivalent function.
Check the SQLite list of core, date/time and aggregate functions.
entries.before: SELECT name, LEN(name) FROM users;
entries.after: SELECT name, length(name) FROM users;
entries.specific: SQLite has no function `{func}`{onLine}.

entries.message: wrong number of arguments to function (?<func>\w+)\(\)
entries.title: wrong number of arguments to function
entries.explain: The function exists, but not with this many arguments. For example `substr` takes 2 or 3, `round` takes 1 or 2, and `length` takes exactly 1.
causes: Leaving out a required argument: `substr(name)`.
An extra argument, often from a misplaced parenthesis or comma.
Using the argument order from another database's version of the function.
fix: Check the function's argument list in the SQLite docs and pass that many.
entries.before: SELECT substr(name) FROM users;
entries.after: SELECT substr(name, 1, 3) FROM users;
entries.specific: `{func}()` is called with the wrong number of arguments{onLine}.

entries.message: SELECTs to the left and right of (?<op>UNION ALL|UNION|INTERSECT|EXCEPT) do not have the same number of result columns
entries.title: SELECTs on each side of UNION have different column counts
entries.explain: `UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` stack the results of two queries, so both must return the same number of columns, matched up by position.
causes: One `SELECT` lists more columns than the other.
`SELECT *` on two tables with different columns.
fix: List the same number of columns on both sides, in the same order.
Fill a missing column with a placeholder: `NULL AS email`.
entries.specific: The two sides of `{op}`{onLine} return different numbers of columns.

entries.title: misuse of window function
entries.explain: Window functions (`ROW_NUMBER()`, `RANK()`, `SUM(...) OVER (...)`) are computed after `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`, so they can appear only in `SELECT` and `ORDER BY`. To filter on them, compute them first in a subquery or CTE.
causes: Filtering on a window function in `WHERE`: `WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1`.
Using one in `GROUP BY` or `HAVING`.
Calling `ROW_NUMBER()` or `RANK()` without an `OVER (...)` clause.
fix: Compute it in a CTE, then filter: `WITH ranked AS (SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) AS rn FROM t) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;`.
Always give window functions an `OVER (...)` clause.
entries.before:
SELECT name FROM scores
WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) = 1;
entries.specific: `{func}()` is used{onLine} where window functions are not allowed.

entries.message: (?<nth>\d+(?:st|nd|rd|th)) (?<clause>ORDER|GROUP) BY term out of range - should be between 1 and (?<max>\d+)
entries.title: ORDER BY term out of range
entries.explain: A plain number in `ORDER BY` or `GROUP BY` means "the Nth column of the result", not a value. The number is larger than the number of columns the `SELECT` returns.
causes: `ORDER BY 3` when the `SELECT` lists only two columns.
Columns were removed from the `SELECT` but the positional `ORDER BY` was not updated.
Meaning to sort by a literal or a column, but writing a number.
fix: Sort by the column name instead of its position: `ORDER BY total DESC`.
Or use a position between 1 and the number of result columns.
entries.before: SELECT name, total FROM orders ORDER BY 3;
entries.after: SELECT name, total FROM orders ORDER BY total DESC;
entries.specific: The {nth} {clause} BY term points past the result's {max} columns{onLine}.

entries.title: sub-select returns N columns - expected 1
entries.explain: A subquery used as a single value, or on the right of `IN`, must return exactly one column. This one returns more.
causes: `WHERE id IN (SELECT id, name FROM ...)`: only the `id` is needed.
A scalar subquery in `SELECT` that lists several columns.
`SELECT *` inside the subquery.
fix: Select only the one column being compared or returned.
If you need several columns from the other table, use a `JOIN` instead.
entries.before:
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id, total FROM orders);
entries.after:
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);
entries.specific: The subquery{onLine} returns {n} columns, but only {expected} is allowed here.

entries.title: no tables specified
entries.explain: `SELECT *` means "all columns of the tables in `FROM`". Without a `FROM` clause there are no tables, so `*` has nothing to expand to.
causes: Forgetting the `FROM` clause.
`SELECT *` used to test an expression without a table.
fix: Add the `FROM table` clause.
To compute a value without a table, select the expression itself: `SELECT 1 + 1;`.
entries.before: SELECT *;
entries.after: SELECT * FROM users;
entries.specific: The `SELECT *`{onLine} has no `FROM` table.
